title: Mu'tah
teaser: An unarmed messenger was beheaded on the Syrian road. Three thousand men went north to answer for him.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: A murdered envoy and an empire's border
layers.content:
Mu'tah is a village on the borders of Greater Syria, a short distance from Baitul-Maqdis. No Muslim army had ever gone that far north. The land beyond it was Byzantine, and Byzantium was reckoned the greatest military power on the earth at that time.

In Jumada al-Ula of the eighth year after the migration, September of 629, al-Harith bin 'Umair al-Azdi rode that road carrying a letter from the Prophet ﷺ to the ruler of Busra. He was intercepted by Shurahbil bin 'Amr al-Ghassani, the governor of al-Balqa' and a close ally of Caesar. Al-Harith was tied, and then he was beheaded.

An envoy was not a soldier. The killing of envoys was regarded as a severe crime, and it amounted to a declaration of war. For more than a year letters had been leaving Madinah for foreign courts, and they had been read, kept, answered, mocked and torn. No bearer had been touched. This was the first.

The Prophet ﷺ was shocked at the news. He ordered an army of three thousand men mobilised and sent north to discipline the transgressors. It was the largest force Madinah had ever put in the field on that scale, except when the Confederates came against the city itself.

Three thousand was a great number for Madinah. Measured against what waited on the other side of the border it was nothing. Al-Mubarakpuri writes that merely thinking of going against Byzantium was considered suicide. Nobody in that column had illusions about the arithmetic. They were not marching out to raid a caravan or reduce a fort. They were marching to the exact patch of ground where one unarmed man had been murdered, to answer for him.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: Three Names in Order
layers.subtitle: A command chain written before they left
layers.content:
Zayd bin Harithah was appointed leader of the army. If Zayd were killed, Ja'far bin Abi Talib was to replace him. If Ja'far were killed too, Abdullah bin Rawahah would succeed him. A white banner was raised and handed to Zayd.

No other expedition had been given its commanders three deep in advance. The order said out loud what everyone had already worked out.

The Prophet ﷺ recommended that when they reached the scene of al-Harith's murder they invite the people to Islam. If they responded, there was to be no fighting. Only if they refused was there any alternative. Then he set the limits: fight in the Name of Allah, neither plunder nor conceal the booty, do not kill any women or children, do not kill an ageing man or a hermit, and neither cut down trees nor demolish homes.

When the preparations were finished the people of Madinah gathered to see the army off. Abdullah bin Rawahah began to weep. Asked why, he swore it was not love for this world or passion for the glamour of life, but the Words of Allah about the Fire that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting. The Prophet ﷺ and the people walked with the army as far as the valley of Thaniyah, and there they were left to the road.

They marched to Ma'an, and at Ma'an the news arrived. Heraclius had come out with a hundred thousand Byzantine troops, and another hundred thousand from the Arab tribes bound to him: Lakhm, Judham, Balqain, Bahra' and Bali. Nobody in the Muslim camp had imagined a number like that. For two nights they argued. Some proposed writing to the Prophet ﷺ and waiting for his instructions.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Banner Changes Hands Four Times
layers.subtitle: What happened on the plain below Masharif
layers.content:
Abdullah bin Rawahah ended the argument. The very object they were trying to avoid, he told them, was the one they had set out seeking: martyrdom. They did not fight counting numbers or equipment, but on the strength of the faith Allah had honoured them with. Hasten, he said, to win either of the two, victory or martyrdom. The army moved.

They met the Byzantines at Masharif, a town of al-Balqa', then changed direction toward Mu'tah and encamped. Qutbah bin Qatadah al-'Udhari led the right flank, Ubadah bin Malik al-Ansari the left. Bitter fighting began: three thousand Muslim soldiers against an enemy the sources put at fifty-fold as large.

Zayd bin Harithah, the closest of them all to the Messenger's heart, held the white banner and fought until he fell, fatally stabbed. Ja'far bin Abi Talib took the leadership. In the thick of the battle he dismounted and killed his own horse, then resumed fighting on foot, which is what a man does when he has decided not to leave. His right hand was severed. He seized the banner with his left, and that was severed too. He clasped it with both arms until a Byzantine soldier struck him and cut him into two parts. Al-Bukhari reported fifty wounds on his body, and not one of them was on his back.

Abdullah bin Rawahah took the banner next and fought on horseback, reciting verses, until he too was killed. The chain of command written out in Madinah was now spent, on one field, in one day.

Then a man of Bani 'Ajlan named Thabit bin al-Arqam lifted the fallen banner, and did not keep it. He called on the Muslims to choose a leader. They chose Khalid bin al-Walid, and the honour was granted unanimously. Al-Bukhari reports that he used and broke nine swords that day.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: No ayah came down; two were already there
layers.content:
No revelation is recorded as having come down about Mu'tah itself. What the sources preserve instead is a verse that had already been sent, and a man who could not stop weeping over it on the day the army left.

The verse Abdullah bin Rawahah had heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting was «وَإِنْ مِنْكُمْ إِلَّا وَارِدُهَا كَانَ عَلَى رَبِّكَ حَتْمًا مَقْضِيًّا» — 'There is not one of you but will pass over it; this is with your Lord, a decree which must be accomplished.' (19:71) He wept at a farewell parade, in front of the whole city, and when they asked him he told them plainly that it was not the enemy and not the leaving. It was that.

The orders he marched under also rest on a verse already given. «وَقَاتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ الَّذِينَ يُقَاتِلُونَكُمْ وَلَا تَعْتَدُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ الْمُعْتَدِينَ» — 'And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed Allah does not love the transgressors.' (2:190) The instructions given at Madinah are that verse itemised: no plunder, no concealed spoils, no women, no children, no ageing man, no hermit, no felled tree, no pulled-down house. They were handed to three thousand men walking toward two hundred thousand, and nothing in them was relaxed for the size of the odds.

One report belongs here rather than on the battlefield. After his death Ja'far was called the flying Ja'far, or Ja'far with two wings, because Allah rewarded him with two wings to fly wherever he wished in the eternal Garden. He lost both arms holding a piece of cloth upright, and the name was given afterwards. He never heard it.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: The defeat that rearranged the whole peninsula
layers.content:
Khalid bin al-Walid did not try to win. He reshuffled the right and left flanks and brought his rear division up to the front so the Byzantines would believe reinforcements had reached the field, held them off in scattered fighting, and pulled the army back in good order. The Byzantines let him go, suspecting a trap in the open desert. Twelve Muslims had been killed. Byzantine losses are unknown, though al-Mubarakpuri notes that the details of the fighting point clearly to a large number.

The objective failed. Al-Harith was not avenged and Shurahbil was not punished. That has to be said before anything else.

But the confrontation itself left a great impression on all the Arabs in Arabia. Tribes that had spent years raiding Madinah — Banu Sulaim, Ashja', Ghatafan, Dhubyan, Fazarah and others — began coming in of their own free will. Farwah bin 'Amr al-Judhami, the Byzantine proxy ruler over the allied Arabs, whose seat was at Ma'an where the army had spent two nights arguing, was moved by what he had seen and became a Muslim, sending a white mule to Madinah with the news. Byzantium imprisoned him, offered him his life if he turned back, and when he refused crucified and beheaded him at a spring called 'Afra' in Palestine. Caesar read the same events and concluded that the Arab tribes now hoped to be free of him, and that Muslim power had to be destroyed before it grew. That is the road to Tabuk.

Carry this. Nothing was gained at Mu'tah. Twelve graves, an unpunished murderer, and an army walking home the way it came. Yet the last expedition the Prophet ﷺ ever ordered was sent to that same border, under Usamah, the son of the Zayd who fell there first. Not one of the men who marched north could see any of that. They were asked only to go forward, in order, when the name before theirs was called.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: What brought the Muslim army north to Mu'tah?

options.text: A Byzantine army had crossed into Arabia
The Prophet's envoy al-Harith bin 'Umair al-Azdi was intercepted and beheaded
A trade caravan from Madinah had been seized at Busra
The Ghassanide tribes had broken a treaty with Madinah

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — al-Harith bin 'Umair al-Azdi was carrying a letter to the ruler of Busra when Shurahbil bin 'Amr al-Ghassani, governor of al-Balqa', had him tied and beheaded.
quiz.scholar_reflection: The killing of envoys was regarded as a severe crime and amounted to a declaration of war. The response was not opportunistic; it was the answer a murdered messenger required.

quiz.prompt: How was the command of the army arranged before it left Madinah?

options.text: Khalid bin al-Walid was appointed leader with Zayd as his deputy
The army was told to elect its own commander on arrival
Zayd bin Harithah led, to be replaced by Ja'far bin Abi Talib, then by Abdullah bin Rawahah
Three commanders shared authority equally over three divisions

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Zayd bin Harithah was appointed leader and given a white banner, Ja'far to replace him if he were killed, and Abdullah bin Rawahah to succeed Ja'far.
quiz.scholar_reflection: No other expedition had its succession written three deep in advance. The order was a forecast, and every man who heard it understood what was being forecast.

quiz.prompt: What does al-Bukhari record about Ja'far bin Abi Talib's body after the battle?

options.text: That it was never recovered from the field
That it bore some fifty wounds, none of them in his back
That he was buried where he fell, at the Prophet's instruction
That he died of his wounds three days after the withdrawal

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — some fifty wounds, and not one of them in his back.
quiz.scholar_reflection: The detail about the back is the whole point of the count. Wounds in front are a record of where a man was facing when each one landed.

quiz.prompt: Thabit bin al-Arqam picked up the banner after the third commander fell. What did he do with it?

options.text: He carried it himself and ordered a general retreat
He called on the Muslims to choose a commander, and they chose Khalid bin al-Walid
He handed it to the commander of the right flank
He sent a rider to Madinah to ask who should take it

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Thabit bin al-Arqam of Bani 'Ajlan raised the fallen banner and called for the appointment of a commander; the choice of Khalid bin al-Walid was unanimous.
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had the banner in his hand and the authority that went with it, and he gave it away in the middle of a battle to the man who could use it better.

quiz.prompt: What were the recorded casualties at Mu'tah?

options.text: Twelve Muslims killed; Byzantine losses are unknown
Seventy Muslims killed; three thousand Byzantines
Twelve Muslims killed; exactly three thousand Byzantines
The sources give no figure for either side

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Muslims suffered twelve martyrs; the number of Byzantine casualties is unknown, though the details of the battle point to a large number.
quiz.scholar_reflection: A source willing to say 'unknown' about the enemy dead is a source worth trusting about the twelve. Round numbers for the other side are usually the first thing invented.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ named three commanders in succession before the army marched. Would you want to be told, out loud and in advance, that your leader is expected to die?

options.text: Yes — an army that knows the plan survives the loss of its leader
No — saying it aloud plants defeat in the ranks before a sword is drawn
Only the officers should know; the rest should be spared it
It changes nothing either way; men fight the same regardless

quiz.slider_label: Name the worst aloud — Keep it from them
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the order of succession from Zayd to Ja'far to Abdullah bin Rawahah was given publicly before departure.
quiz.scholar_reflection: The chain held for exactly as long as it needed to. Three men died and the banner never touched the ground, because the answer to 'who now' had been settled a month earlier in Madinah.

quiz.prompt: Three thousand men were sent against two hundred thousand under orders not to cut a tree, harm a hermit, or pull down a house. Should rules of restraint bend when the odds are that bad?

options.text: No — rules that bend under pressure were never rules
Yes — survival outranks etiquette when you are outnumbered fifty to one
They should hold for civilians but not for property
The commander on the ground should decide, not the man who stayed home

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the marching orders forbade plunder, concealed booty, killing women, children, ageing men and hermits, felling trees and demolishing homes.
quiz.scholar_reflection: The limits were set by the same authority that ordered the march. A soldier who can be talked out of them by arithmetic is carrying someone else's orders.

quiz.prompt: Abdullah bin Rawahah wept at the farewell — not over the enemy, but over an ayah about the Fire. What does that tell you about what he was actually afraid of?

options.text: That the battle had stopped frightening him and something larger had not
That fear of the unseen and fear of the sword are the same fear in different clothes
That he was grieving the city and the verse gave him a reason he could say out loud
That a man who weeps in public has already made peace with dying

quiz.slider_label: Fear the field — Fear the verse
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — he swore his weeping was not for love of this world or the glamour of life, but for the Words of Allah in 19:71 that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ recite.
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was asked in front of a whole city and he answered precisely. He then went north as the third name in a chain of command and told two thousand nine hundred men to hasten toward it.

quiz.prompt: Khalid bin al-Walid dressed a retreat up as a reinforcement and walked the army out. Was that a commander's success or a commander's failure?

options.text: A success — he brought back an army that should not have come back
A failure — the ground was abandoned and the murder went unanswered
Neither; it was the only move on the board and any commander would have found it
A success in the field and a failure in the mission, and the two do not cancel

quiz.slider_label: Hold the ground — Bring them home
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Khalid reshuffled the flanks, moved the rear division forward to suggest reinforcements, and withdrew the army in order; the Byzantines suspected a desert trap and broke off.
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had been elected an hour earlier by men standing over three dead commanders. What he did with the hour was decide that the army was worth more than the field.

quiz.prompt: Mu'tah did not achieve what it was sent to achieve, and it changed Arabia anyway. Which do you judge an action by?

options.text: The objective — anything else is consolation after the fact
The effect — the peninsula reorganised itself around what those men did
The intention, since neither objective nor effect is fully in anyone's hands
The cost — twelve graves is the only figure that is certain

quiz.slider_label: Judge the objective — Judge the effect
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Muslims could not avenge al-Harith, yet the confrontation left a great impression on all the Arabs in Arabia, and tribes including Banu Sulaim, Ashja', Ghatafan, Dhubyan and Fazarah came to accept Islam of their own free will.
quiz.scholar_reflection: Farwah bin 'Amr al-Judhami watched the losing side and changed sides, then died for it at a spring in Palestine. He is the clearest evidence that whatever happened at Mu'tah, defeat is not the word for it.
